items.rss_description: Pricing at the Speed of the Market Emerging Technologies RyanMeyer Wed, 10/28/2026 - 11:33 As loss costs shift and new risks emerge, modern insurance pricing platforms are shortening the path from insight to price and changing how pricing works with underwriting. November 11, 1111 Image Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Kumarappan Sundaram Pricing is moving from a periodic project to a continuous capability. With catastrophe volatility and shifting market conditions, treating pricing as an occasional exercise is hard to sustain. Two shifts stand out. First, dedicated pricing platforms. Rating, models and rules increasingly sit on purpose-built platforms rather than inside the core policy system. Second, modern software discipline. Version control, automated testing and continual monitoring of live models are becoming standard. Paul Carroll What is driving carriers to invest in sophisticated pricing platforms now? Kumarappan Sundaram Five things. First, speed-to-market of rate changes. Moving from quarterly or annual releases, gated by IT and policy admin deployment, to something near-continuous is the key value. Decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is also a practical starting point for core modernization, delivering value without an entire core replacement. Second, loss cost volatility and trend uncertainty. Social inflation, repair and parts costs, tariffs and secondary-peril catastrophe losses make trend assumptions go stale faster. Carriers want faster feedback from emerging claims experience that they can incorporate into price. Third, segment-level control. Carriers want to grow where they are well priced and hold the line where they are not, which means testing, deploying and monitoring changes at a granular level. Fourth, regulatory and governance demands. Filing, documentation and explainability requirements keep growing. Audit trails can be far easier to build in than to retrofit. Fifth, data ecosystem expansion. Telematics, geospatial and property-level data, cat model output and third-party enrichment should flow into rating at quote speed, which can often be the real integration challenge. A CFO will often ask how the benefit is measured, so programs should define measurement up front. Paul Carroll Underwriting and pricing are tightly linked conceptually, but loosely coupled in practice. Why is that, and can they be brought into phase? Kumarappan Sundaram The link is strong in theory but weak in practice, mainly for technology and operating-model reasons. Start with systems and data. Pricing logic sits in a rating engine or pricing platform, while underwriters work in a different workbench based on the data in the submission, so the two rarely share a view of the risk. Then there are different rhythms. Pricing changes on a release cycle, while underwriting decisions are made submission by submission. Overrides and discounts help fill the gap. Finally, the feedback loop is weak. Why underwriters override a price rarely flows back to pricing in a structured way, so a valuable signal is lost. Modern pricing platforms increasingly aim to close this gap. Bringing them into phase is mainly an integration and governance task. Pricing can be exposed as a service that the underwriting workbench calls in real time, connected to appetite, distribution, retention and claims signals. Overrides can be captured as data, and authority and guardrails can be made explicit. In complex commercial risks, underwriter judgment legitimately plays a larger role, so the aim there is visibility and learning, not automation. Paul Carroll How can modern pricing technology help carriers price emerging risks? Kumarappan Sundaram Emerging risks, such as cyber, climate-related perils and new auto and energy technologies, may not come with deep loss history. A modern platform helps in four ways. First, new data sources as proxies. Outside-in cyber scans, geospatial and property-level data, and vehicle and telematics data give carriers signals where claims history is thin. The platform brings them together with internal experience and subject matter specialist judgment, with clear rules for how the weighting shifts as claims data builds. Second, scenario testing. Teams can test prices against stress scenarios, such as a major catastrophe or a systemic cyber event. Third, fast, controlled learning. Small, measured changes show what a new risk is worth sooner and with less exposure than a book-wide change. Fourth, flexible product design. Configurable rating makes it easier to adjust deductibles, sublimits and endorsements as understanding of the risk develops. The limit can be that technology cannot create data that does not exist. For novel risks, the platform helps carriers learn and adjust quickly, alongside accumulation controls, reinsurance and underwriting oversight. Paul Carroll What impact is AI having on pricing and rating, and where should leaders be skeptical? Kumarappan Sundaram I would separate what is emerging with clear value from what is still unproven. The clearest near-term value is GenAI around the pricing process. The more underrated opportunity is in the work surrounding the price: drafting and reconciling rate filings, translating pricing specifications into platform configuration, documenting changes, summarizing competitor filings and preparing data. These steps slow the path to market, and errors are easier to review than in a pricing decision itself. What is still unproven is AI acting on pricing decisions. The idea of agents that monitor performance, propose rate actions and test them is compelling. But pricing is regulated and auditable, and many carriers are not ready for autonomous rate changes. For now, I expect AI to propose and people to approve, so the quality of that review is the real control. As AI capabilities become widely available, proprietary data, speed of deployment and governance are likely to matter more as differentiators. Carriers that treat AI as a standalone upgrade, without the platform and operating model underneath it, risk building capability they cannot put into production. Paul Carroll What would you advise a carrier to do first? Kumarappan Sundaram Measure your cycle time, from the point a pricing change is approved to the point it is live throughout the various channels. Many carriers have never seen that number, and it shows where value is being lost. Then prioritize platform and process changes that shorten it. Put governance in place before scaling AI, and start with one or two lines where faster pricing has a clear, measurable payoff. Resist modernizing everything at once. Paul Carroll Thanks. This is all super helpful. -- Kumarappan (Kumar) Sundaram is a Managing Director in PwC’s Property and Casualty Operations and Technology practice and a leader of its Insurance Core Transformation and Pricing/Rating offering. With more than two decades of consulting experience, he partners with US and UK P&C carriers, from large international insurers to small regional ones, across personal, commercial, and specialty lines, with depth in commercial and specialty. He has led numerous large-scale programs modernizing policy, claims, and pricing/rating operations, and works with PwC’s strategy, management, technology, and actuarial teams to deliver integrated solutions, thought leadership, and sales. -- Sponsored by PwC Insurance Thought Leadership ITL Partner: PwC

items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.title: Go Beyond the Flow
items.original_title: Go Beyond the Flow
items.rss_title: Go Beyond the Flow
items.rss_description: Go Beyond the Flow Leadership ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 09:32 Workflow platforms boost efficiency, but synchronous interaction builds the social capital that makes digital collaboration truly effective. Excerpted from "Social Capital at Work." November 3, 2026 Image Collaboration. It's what every leader hopes for in her team. It's the purpose behind much of our communication at work. And it can be a challenge. There is a collaboration platform in the digital workplace for almost everything. Salesforce. Asana. HubSpot. Figma. Git. ServiceNow. Too many to name them all. Each tracks and assigns work items and enables us to collaborate through a system. The systems sit between us. They enable us to tell one another what to do online. Want something done, open a ticket. Want to feel productive, pound through your task list, and assign "work items" to the next person in the workflow. Fire, then forget. Most of the time, this works just fine. The efficiency can't be disputed. But ask yourself a couple of questions. Are there times you assign a task in Salesforce and get back a result you didn't expect? Have you ever opened an Asana task and not known what you were being asked to do? Our experience tells us it happens all the time. Communication scholars and system architects make a distinction between synchronous and asynchronous messages. Synchronous communications occur in real time and involve immediate back and forth between participants. Asynchronous communications allow for time delays. Workflow assignments are asynchronous. They happen independent of an immediate response. Sometimes, in fact, responses don't happen at all. Workflow makes it easy to make an ask of a colleague, assign a task to a subordinate, offer feedback to a collaborator. They also eliminate the synchronicity of a person-to-person "handoff." Evidence suggests synchronous interaction makes us feel connected at work. It even fosters relationships, which make asynchronous communication on workflow platforms more effective. An intriguing study of software engineers proves it. The engineers worked in two buildings several blocks apart. In some instances, teams worked together in the same building. In others, the team members were spread across the locations. As is common in the software industry, the engineers used a platform to share code, give one another assignments, and provide feedback. Researchers found that teams of engineers working in the same building—that is, colleagues who had frequent synchronous interactions with one another—received 23% more online feedback—an asynchronous interaction—on their code than did those on multi-building teams whose members had less frequent face-to-face contact with one another. "Sitting near workers increases not only in-person but also digital collaboration," the authors write. The collocated software engineers enjoyed the benefits of social capital: mentorship, coaching, learning, and collaboration. All were achieved through a digital tool that, when coupled with the opportunity for synchronous interaction, worked for and not against social capital. Everyone benefited, especially those newest to the team. Retention among newer joiners was significantly higher among collocated teams than dispersed teams. Young workers and women, the authors tell us, are "substantially more likely to quit the firm when they lose proximity to coworkers." Less feedback. Less connection. Lesser results. It's a lesson the system architects at Amwins, led by Ben Sloop, took to heart when they designed their collaboration platform. Ben knows his way around a spreadsheet. A boardroom, too. Harvard undergrad. Stanford MBA. A stint as a management consultant at Bain, then a few years in private equity. The perfect pedigree for his current role as president and chief operating officer of Amwins, the nation's largest wholesale insurance broker. But there's more to Ben's success than his stellar resume. Ben told us, "One of the core requirements to gain more responsibility here is having deep, real relationships with our salespeople. I spend a disproportionate amount of my time talking to and staying connected with people in the field. Of all the people that I'll respond to, first is if one of our brokers reaches out to me. That's the top of my inbox." Amwins' clients are retail insurance brokers and agents looking to find homes for complex, hard-to-place risks—think workers' compensation insurance for circus performers. The insurance carriers who advertise on the Super Bowl don't want the hard stuff. And so, retail brokers work with wholesalers like Amwins to get complex risks placed with one of a large legion of specialty insurance carriers. Each occupies a well-defined niche within the commercial insurance market. Each is expert in a particular type of risk. This creates a classic many-to-many problem. Thousands of customers, thousands of carriers and thousands of Amwins brokers sitting between them. The challenge is having the right expertise at the right time. "Our brokers have to be specialists," Ben told us. "Our retailers don't want to work with someone that does everything a little bit, because that's kind of what they do. They want to deal with someone that's a deep expert." Enabling his brokers to always find that one expert within their large, decentralized organization became a key part of Amwins' founding mission. It's the hardest part of what they do, Ben told us. "In order to be a deep expert, what that means is that, well, if my client comes to me and they ask me for a construction wrap policy in Scottsdale that I know nothing about, I've got to know where to get them what they need inside our own firm. So, we don't lose that client, right? And so, this created this huge coordination problem." The company built Amlink to solve it. Amlink is the wholesaler's proprietary relationship management system. It is a workflow platform, but it's different. Ben beamed with a creator's pride as he told us how it works. "I can look in the system and say, well, actually, we have a guy who lives in Scottsdale and does only construction wraps, right? And so, I can reach out to that person who I usually know personally, because we have all sorts of sales events. The point is to build connectivity with an internal coordination mechanism." We both have seen lots of systems that tried to solve similar problems. All did it the same way. Type in "construction wrap in Scottsdale" and you'd get deal listings, PowerPoint presentations, maybe a white paper or two. Lots of stuff to wade through, maybe some good slides you can reuse, but probably not the answer you need. Amlink is different. It delivers names and contact information and forces conversations to happen. It's effective at both delivering expertise when it's needed and building relationships across the firm. Knowing who to turn to can make or break a deal. Amwins brokers don't just compete on expertise—they compete on connectedness. Amlink is a unicorn. "I've never seen another system in the industry like this. Everyone says it's a people business. but they tend not to track [data] at the people level," Ben told us. He was clear to put the tech in its proper context: "We are a technology-enabled business. The thoughtful use of technology makes our people better. But we are fundamentally a person-to-person business." Social capital matters at Amwins. It drives market results. It also creates an environment where people want to stay. "You know, it's funny. I joined 19 years ago, and I still think of myself as one of the newer people," Ben confessed, explaining that Amwins was the kind of place "good people stay for a long time. People typically don't leave just for money. People tend to leave because they just don't feel connected, don't like who they're working with, don't feel compelled by the strategy." We probably should have introduced you to Ben at the very beginning. " Social Capital at Work ," by John Burrows and Seth Rachlin, will be published by Simon Acumen on Nov. 10. This article is excerpted from their book. John Burrows Seth Rachlin

The perfect pedigree for his current role as president and chief operating officer of Amwins, the nation's largest wholesale insurance broker. But there's more to Ben's success than his stellar resume. Ben told us, "One of the core requirements to gain more responsibility here is having deep, real relationships with our salespeople. I spend a disproportionate amount of my time talking to and staying connected with people in the field. Of all the people that I'll respond to, first is if one of our brokers reaches out to me. That's the top of my inbox." Amwins' clients are retail insurance brokers and agents looking to find homes for complex, hard-to-place risks—think workers' compensation insurance for circus performers. The insurance carriers who advertise on the Super Bowl don't want the hard stuff. And so, retail brokers work with wholesalers like Amwins to get complex risks placed with one of a large legion of specialty insurance carriers. Each occupies a well-defined niche within the commercial insurance market. Each is expert in a particular type of risk. This creates a classic many-to-many problem. Thousands of customers, thousands of carriers and thousands of Amwins brokers sitting between them. The challenge is having the right expertise at the right time. "Our brokers have to be specialists," Ben told us. "Our retailers don't want to work with someone that does everything a little bit, because that's kind of what they do. They want to deal with someone that's a deep expert." Enabling his brokers to always find that one expert within their large, decentralized organization became a key part of Amwins' founding mission. It's the hardest part of what they do, Ben told us. "In order to be a deep expert, what that means is that, well, if my client comes to me and they ask me for a construction wrap policy in Scottsdale that I know nothing about, I've got to know where to get them what they need inside our own firm. So, we don't lose that client, right? And so, this created this huge coordination problem." The company built Amlink to solve it. Amlink is the wholesaler's proprietary relationship management system. It is a workflow platform, but it's different. Ben beamed with a creator's pride as he told us how it works. "I can look in the system and say, well, actually, we have a guy who lives in Scottsdale and does only construction wraps, right? And so, I can reach out to that person who I usually know personally, because we have all sorts of sales events. The point is to build connectivity with an internal coordination mechanism." We both have seen lots of systems that tried to solve similar problems. All did it the same way. Type in "construction wrap in Scottsdale" and you'd get deal listings, PowerPoint presentations, maybe a white paper or two. Lots of stuff to wade through, maybe some good slides you can reuse, but probably not the answer you need. Amlink is different. It delivers names and contact information and forces conversations to happen. It's effective at both delivering expertise when it's needed and building relationships across the firm. Knowing who to turn to can make or break a deal. Amwins brokers don't just compete on expertise—they compete on connectedness. Amlink is a unicorn. "I've never seen another system in the industry like this. Everyone says it's a people business. but they tend not to track [data] at the people level," Ben told us. He was clear to put the tech in its proper context: "We are a technology-enabled business. The thoughtful use of technology makes our people better. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.extracted_text: Insurers urged to adapt reinsurance structures as secondary peril losses climb: Marsh Re - Artemis.bm Insurers urged to adapt reinsurance structures as secondary peril losses climb: Marsh Re - Artemis.bm Insurers urged to adapt reinsurance structures as secondary peril losses climb: Marsh Re 5th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As insured losses arising from secondary perils, such as severe convective storms, wildfire, winter storms and flood, continue to be a major contributor to insured catastrophe losses in North America, reinsurance broker Marsh Re has outlined that this shift is placing greater pressure on insurers to reassess their reinsurance arrangements. In a recently published report, Marsh Re, underlines that conventional reinsurance strategies have not fully adjusted to this shift, as many programmes, models, and pricing frameworks continuing to prioritise protection against rare, large-scale catastrophic events, rather than recurring, less severe events. The broker outlines that disconnect has created a “fundamental strategic challenge for insurers,” and that closing the gap is fast becoming a way for insurers to stand out from competitors. US-insured severe convective storm losses have exceeded $30 billion a year every year since 2020, and topped $40 billion in four of those years, Marsh Re’s report stated. At the same time, the broker also highlighted that the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfire produced the largest insured wildfire loss on record. Marsh Re also indicated that a season of 15 midsize hail events can do more damage to an insurer’s income statement than the one-in-100-year hurricane that still anchors many capital models. Importantly, this problem has heavily grown since the 2023 reinsurance market reset, which pushed retentions higher. The broker said that this development has reduced the proportion of catastrophe claims absorbed by reinsurers, which has caused for more of the cost of these frequent, smaller events to fall on primary insurers’ balance sheets. Additionally, Marsh Re noted that catastrophe models for secondary perils continue to improve but stressed that validation remains uneven. The broker’s testing found that model loss estimates can shift materially from one release to the next, and results for the same portfolio can vary widely, especially in less mature areas, such as urban conflagration. Kim Roberts, North American Peril Advisory Leader, Marsh Re, and author of the report, commented: “The insurers that outperform over the next cycle will be the ones that bring the same discipline to hail, wildfire, and winter storm that they apply to capital planning and reinsurance strategy. That means knowing where their portfolios are most exposed, validating models against their own claims experience, and structuring protection around repeated midsize losses, not just the rare peak event.” As part of its recommendations, Marsh Re suggests that insurers combine vendor model output with their own claims experience and validate results before using them to make decisions. The broker also calls for better exposure-level mitigation data, from roof age and construction to community resilience measures, to help sharpen risk views. Marsh Re also suggests that insurers review the design of their reinsurance programs around the accumulation of losses, through annual aggregate covers, second-event reinsurance layers and low-attaching structures. Marsh Re also acknowledged that obtaining these structures at acceptable prices is difficult for some insurers across the market. The broker also indicated that access to reinsurance capacity will increasingly depend on the quality of insurers’ exposure assessments and will go to portfolios which effectively demonstrate that risks are modeled accurately and completely. It’s important to remember that both the catastrophe bond and broader insurance-linked securities (ILS) market continue to provide aggregate reinsurance and retrocession capacity, where programs are well structured, the terms of coverage are appropriate and balanced between parties, and pricing is deemed to be reasonable. items.extracted_text: Swiss Re's P&C reinsurance result delivers, despite competitive market weighing - Artemis.bm Swiss Re's P&C reinsurance result delivers, despite competitive market weighing - Artemis.bm Swiss Re’s P&C reinsurance result delivers, despite competitive market weighing 5th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Swiss Re has reported on-target results for its property and casualty (P&C) reinsurance division for the first nine months of this year, as lower than anticipated natural catastrophe losses and strong underwriting performance both served to offset the effects of the competitive and softened market environment. Swiss Re reported that its P&C reinsurance division delivered insurance revenue of $12.8 billion for 2026 so far, which is bang on analyst consensus for the company. But as soft market conditions weigh, this was down on the $14 billion from the prior year, due to “overall renewals outcome and reduced volumes written by cedents,” the company explained. But, with a combined ratio of just 77.3%, which beat the analyst consensus of 78.5%, Swiss Re still managed to deliver $2.2 billion of net income in the P&C reinsurance division, only 6% down on 9-month 2025. However, where competitive and softer reinsurance market conditions are most evident is in Swiss Re’s new business contractual service margin (CSM), which reflects the profitability of new business under written in the period. For P&C reinsurance this came in at $1.8 billion for Swiss Re, down meaningfully from $2.5 billion in the prior year, which the company said is reflective of “a competitive year-to-date market environment.” As we all know, the competition is likely to get even fiercer going forwards, while pricing is expected to soften further as well, meaning the profitability of new underwriting business will likely decline further across the reinsurance sector. Swiss Re’s CFO Anders Malmström commented during a media call this morning, “Our discussions with market participants confirmed that market conditions vary significantly by geography and line of business. “Pricing pressure is generally greater in markets with fewer losses, particularly in property nat cat, while additional capital is increasing capacity and competition. “Our teams are well prepared to navigate the current market dynamics. We are staying close to our clients and brokers, identifying attractive opportunities, and supporting them not only with capacity, but more importantly with our expertise and solutions.” Lower natural catastrophe losses have also helped Swiss Re’s result, in addition to which a higher contribution from life and health reinsurance offset the impact of competitive P&C conditions for the company. Large natural catastrophe losses reached $640 million and man-made losses $301 million for the first nine months of 2026. The nat cat loss budget was higher and the consensus for nat cat was also higher at $649 million. Across the group, Swiss Re has reported a net income of $1.3 billion for Q3 2026, net income of $4.2 billion and a return on equity (ROE) of 22.5% for the first nine months of the year. Both of the net income figures are again above the analysts consensus figures. Swiss Re’s Group Chief Executive Officer Andreas Berger commented, “Our result for the first nine months reflects disciplined underwriting and the deliberate decisions we have made over recent quarters to strengthen our portfolio and build a more resilient business. We are applying the same long-term approach as P&C market conditions shift, combining underwriting discipline and greater cost efficiency with commercial ambition, working closely with clients and brokers to identify attractive opportunities. At a time when risks are becoming increasingly complex and interconnected, Swiss Re is well positioned to support clients with the expertise, capacity and solutions they ask for.” Group Chief Financial Officer Anders Malmström added, “Our strong current earnings reflect disciplined underwriting and portfolio management, while lower margins on new business reflect the competitive P&C pricing environment we are seeing today. Our focus on simplifying Swiss Re and directing resources where they create the greatest value is bringing us closer to clients and driving progress towards our cost reduction targets. At the same time, L&H Re’s large in-force portfolio, consistently strong performance from Corporate Solutions and healthy recurring investment income continue to provide important support to Group profitability. From a capital management perspective, the execution of our USD 1.5 billion share buyback programme, announced in February, is nearly complete.” Looking ahead, Berger added, “We maintain our two priorities: delivering on our financial targets and the Group’s overall resilience. Our performance in the first nine months puts us firmly on track to meet both goals. Looking beyond 2026, our robust foundations and the diversification provided by our three Business Units give us confidence in our ability to navigate different market cycles successfully. items.extracted_text: Cat bond risk spreads fall to lowest level since 2017, as tightening continued in October: Plenum - Artemis.bm Cat bond risk spreads fall to lowest level since 2017, as tightening continued in October: Plenum - Artemis.bm Cat bond risk spreads fall to lowest level since 2017, as tightening continued in October: Plenum 5th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Catastrophe bond insurance risk spreads declined further in October 2026, as seasonal tightening continued to affect the overall yield of the cat bond market. Cat bond risk spreads now stand at their lowest since 2017 and while the tightening trend will end soon, it remains to be seen how lower spreads of new issuance affect the market yield going forwards. The latest data on cat bond yields from Plenum Investments shows that the typical hurricane seasonal spread tightening continued last month, while with new issuance picking up again the expected loss of the cat bond market had increased in October as well. As a result, by October 30th, the overall coupon yield of the catastrophe bond market had fallen to 8.41%, which is down from the September 25th figure of 8.74%. The insurance risk spread of the outstanding cat bond market now stands at 4.33% at October 30th 2026, which is down roughly 13% on the same time last year. The last time cat bond market risk spreads fell this low was in August 2017, according to Plenum Investments’ data, although it’s worth noting that was after they had increased from as low as 3.3% in November 2016. The overall cat bond market coupon yield of 8.41% is down approximately 4.5%, less of a decline than insurance risk spreads alone due to the fact the USD money market rate was lower a year ago. It’s worth considering though that the expected loss of the cat bond market was measured at 2.25% on October 31st 2025, but by October 30th 2026 this stood at 2.55%, showing a little more risk is being assumed due to the profile of catastrophe bonds in the outstanding market at this time. Click the chart below to analyse the interactive data : Plenum Investments commented on the end of October update, “Total returns in the CAT bond market varied by currency, ranging from 8.4% (previous month: 8.7%) in USD, to 7.0% in EUR (previous month: 7.2%), and 4.2% in CHF (previous month: 4.5%). “Spread tightening continued in October, with spreads narrowing by a further 5%. However, the pace of tightening is slowing, as expected towards the end of the hurricane season. This trend is likely to persist at a more moderate pace into November, before spreads are expected to start widening again in December.” While spread widening is expected to begin again given the seasonality of premiums and returns in the catastrophe bond market, as we said the question is how the market yield bounces back given the inclusion of lower-priced cat bonds issued during this softer phase of the market cycle. While seasonality affects the insurance risk spread of the cat bond market, so too does the average spread across all deals outstanding and so newer issues will begin to increasingly show in the data. They are already showing the in expected loss of the cat bond market, which has risen in recent weeks. Although we should also note that maturities also affect that metric, as the composition of the cat bond market changes. With the cat bond market pipeline now building steadily and fourth-quarter looking to be another strong period of issuance, greater visibility of how new issues affect market metrics will be visible in the coming month or two. It’s also important to remember the contribution of the risk-free return on collateral, which boosts overall coupon yields considerably for the cat bond market. When risk spreads bottomed out in 2016, the total yield of the catastrophe bond market, or the coupon available to cat bond investors, fell to as low as around 3.70%. Today, the collateral yield is 4.08% on its own, so added to a 4.33% risk spread gives the total coupon return of 8.41% as of now. Looking at the catastrophe bond market’s return over expected loss, so the expected excess return of sorts, today that stands at 5.86% as of October 30th, down from 6.24% as of September 25th. But, in the depths of the soft reinsurance market in 2016 when cat bond risk spreads hit their lowest-level ever, even with the expected loss being lower at that time, the cat bond market yield over expected loss was actually below 2%. So, comparably, spreads and yields of the catastrophe bond market are much higher today than they fell to in the last soft reinsurance market. With catastrophe bonds still seen as a beneficial diversifier and source of relatively uncorrelated returns for investment portfolios, it’s perhaps no surprise investor appetite remains strong, even as pricing has fallen. items.extracted_text: Selective returns for catastrophe bond renewal, with $300m High Point Re 2027-1 - Artemis.bm Selective returns for catastrophe bond renewal, with $300m High Point Re 2027-1 - Artemis.bm Selective returns for catastrophe bond renewal, with $300m High Point Re 2027-1 5th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Selective Insurance Company is back in the catastrophe bond market for is second sponsorship, seeking $300 million or more in multi-peril collateralized reinsurance from a High Point Re Ltd. (Series 2027-1) issuance that will renew and expand coverage from its soon to mature first deal, sources have explained. Selective Insurance, the US property and casualty insurer, had sponsored its debut catastrophe bond back in 2023, securing $300 million of protection from the High Point Re Ltd. (Series 2023-1) issuance. That cat bond cover matures at the end of this year. That debut cat bond sponsorship, protected Selective Insurance against losses from multiple US perils, but excluded coverage for the states of California, Florida, Louisiana and Texas. However, this new High Point Re 2027-1 cat bond will include coverage for all 50 US states and DC, we understand, showing Selective’s expansion and desire to benefit from reinsurance across all exposed regions. So this new catastrophe bond targets both a renewal and an expansion of the capital markets backed coverage for the company, it appears. High Point Re Ltd., a Bermuda based special purpose insurer (SPI), is targeting issuance of a single $300 million tranche of Series 2027-1 Class A notes, which will be sold to investors and the proceeds used to collateralize a multi-year and multi-peril reinsurance agreement with the sponsor Selective Insurance Company. The cat bond notes that High Point Re Ltd. is offering are designed to provide Selective and subsidiaries with a four year source of reinsurance to the end of 2030, covering it against losses from U.S. named storms, earthquakes, severe thunderstorms, winter storms, wildfires, meteorite impacts and volcanic eruptions across the United States, we understand. That reinsurance will provide its protection on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis, sources said, with the targeted $300 million or greater tranche of Class A notes attaching their reinsurance protection from an $800 million loss and covering a share of losses up to $1.5 billion for Selective. As a result, the High Point Re Series 2027-1 Class A cat bond notes will come with an initial attachment probability of 0.93%, an initial base expected loss of 0.6% and we are told they are being offered to investors with price guidance for a spread in a range from 2.75% to 3.25%. We can compare that to the High Point Re 2023-1 cat bond , which was issued with an initial base expected loss of 0.77% and priced to pay investors a spread of 5.75%. As a result, the multiple-at-market once again looks meaningfully lower with this new cat bond, given the much softer reinsurance market pricing conditions at this point in the cycle. It’s encouraging to see Selective Insurance returning to renew its catastrophe bond protection. It will be interesting to see whether the company looks to upsize this deal, given the wide layer of its reinsurance tower that the notes will participate in. items.extracted_text: MS Amlin syndicate targets $100m aggregate retro with Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm MS Amlin syndicate targets $100m aggregate retro with Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm MS Amlin syndicate targets $100m aggregate retro with Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond 5th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Lloyd’s syndicate 2001, which is aligned with Mitsui Sumitomo underwriting entity MS Amlin, is seeking its first catastrophe bond protection, with a $100 million target for multi-peril and multi-regional retrocession from an Arthur Re Ltd. – Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond sponsorship, Artemis has learned. As the name suggests, this is another industry-loss triggered catastrophe bond being issued through the Gallagher Re operated Arthur Re Ltd. platform that helps make issuance of industry-loss index trigger cat bonds more cost effective and efficient. We’re told the ceding entity to this catastrophe bond is Lloyd’s syndicate 2001, with the coverage also set to benefit sub-syndicate 1673, both of which are managed by MS Amlin Underwriting Limited and underwrite for the MS Amlin arm of the global Mitsui Sumitomo insurance group. We’ve not seen an Amlin entity in the catastrophe bond market since 2014, when Amlin AG sponsored the last of the Tramline Re series of deals. Since then of course, Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance acquired Amlin back in 2016. While we have regularly seen Mitsui Sumitomo itself and entities of MS&AD Holdings sponsor cat bonds, for Japanese reinsurance protection, we have not seen MS Amlin entities linked to cat bonds, so this should be considered another first-time sponsor entrant to the catastrophe bond market. For this cat bond issuance for the MS Amlin linked Syndicate 2001 and sub-syndicate 1673, Arthur Re Ltd. is offering what we’re told is currently targeted to be a $100 million tranche of Class A notes to investors on behalf of a segregated account named Kanata Re 2026-1. The Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond notes from Arthur Re are designed to provide Syndicate 2001 and sub-entities with a multi-year source of fully-collateralized multi-peril and multi-regional retrocessional reinsurance from the capital markets. That protection will be on an annual aggregate and industry loss index trigger basis, while the covered perils and regions are U.S. named storm, U.S. and Canada earthquake and European windstorm events. The protection is designed to run across a four-year term with four calendar year annual aggregate risk periods, we understand, from the start of 2027 to the end of 2030. The $100 million of Kanata Re 2026-1 cat bond notes will feature franchise deductibles of $10 million for named storms, $25 million for earthquakes and $6 million for European windstorm events, we are told. The Class A notes would attach their coverage at $600 million and exhaust their coverage at $700 million. items.extracted_text: LA Port Strike Risk Pushed to Friday as Labor Talks Continue Article 0 Comments The union representing about 250 security workers at the U.S.’s biggest seaports agreed to extend a contract negotiation deadline until midnight Friday, their employers said. With the extension comes a renewed strike threat that could impact operations at several terminals across the Port of Long Beach and the Port of Los Angeles if no deal is reached. “Negotiations will continue on Friday with the help of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service,” the Pacific Maritime Association said in a statement on Wednesday evening. “PMA remains committed to reaching a fair agreement at the bargaining table that avoids disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports.” The International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 represents watchmen employed at terminals responsible for about more than half of the combined cargo at the Southern California ports, according to the PMA. ILWU Local 26 President Luisa Gratz did not return a request for comment. The PMA, which represents port terminals and ocean carriers, warned on Oct. 27 that ILWU dockworkers and marine clerks — who have separate labor contracts and are not party to this dispute — are expected to stand with the watchmen in the event of a strike. items.title: Miami Beach Buildings Sinking at Different Rates, Due to Construction, Study Finds
items.original_title: Miami Beach Buildings Sinking at Different Rates, Due to Construction, Study Finds
items.rss_title: Miami Beach Buildings Sinking at Different Rates, Due to Construction, Study Finds
items.rss_description: Much of the Miami Beach skyline, on ground that’s just a few feet above sea level, is sinking. But some of the iconic skyscrapers there are sinking at different rates and much of the subsidence is due to non-stop building …
items.extracted_text: Miami Beach Buildings Sinking at Different Rates, Due to Construction, Study Finds Article 0 Comments Much of the Miami Beach skyline, on ground that’s just a few feet above sea level, is sinking. But some of the iconic skyscrapers there are sinking at different rates and much of the subsidence is due to non-stop building construction on the barrier island, says a study led by professors from Florida and German universities. “We attribute the observed subsidence to load-induced, prolonged creep deformation of the sandy layers within the limestone, which is accelerated, if not instigated, by construction activities,” reads the abstract for a study published in Earth and Space Science , a peer-reviewed academic journal. The study , authored in part by University of Miami professors Farzaneh Aziz Zanjani and Falk Amelung, was published in late 2024. But it has gained new attention after it was was highlighted in recent news articles in the Miami Herald and other publications. Red shows subsidence from 2016 to 2023. Orange is for 2019 to 2023. From the study. Click to enlarge. The authors of the study used satellite-based Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar, known as InSAR, to document the sink rate for 35 Miami Beach buildings over the last decade. The findings show that some structures have sunk into the ancient limestone and sand beneath them at a rate of about 2 centimeters from 2016 to 2023. But others, on Sunny Isles Beach and Surfside, have dropped more than 8 centimeters, or about three inches, raising new concerns for insurance underwriters and claims handlers. The sinking structures include the famous, 60-story Porche Design Tower, which has seen many complaints from residents about cracking and leaking, and Trump Tower III, which is settling at almost a centimeter per year. Some subsidence is expected for most skyscrapers, and it usually ceases shortly after construction, according to news reports. But the sink rate on parts of crowded Miami Beach barrier islands suggest the sink rate is worsening. More recent subsidence measurements correlate to construction-induced problems. It’s probable that differential rates of subsidence could lead to exacerbated structural issues and more insurance claims. “There are no indications that subsidence will come to a stop,” the study concludes. “For structures subsiding at a constant rate this is obvious. For structures exhibiting a true exponential decay in subsidence, it could eventually cease. However, nearby construction vibrations are likely to restart the grain rearrangement process, leading to a renewed acceleration of subsidence.” The study noted that Champlain Towers South, which collapsed in 2021, killing 98 people, showed no signs of subsidence before the disaster. Engineering reports have blamed the collapse mostly on deteriorated support columns at the 40-year-old condominium building. But the recent subsidence study noted that the 87 Park tower adjacent to the Champlain Tower site is showing signs of sinking. And “subsidence of nearby low-rise buildings with relatively small structural loads … is almost certainly driven by construction activities,” the study concluded. The Herald reported that it reached out to managers of all buildings cited in the study, but all declined to comment. The city of Sunny Isles Beach officials said last year that they had seen no reports of damage associated with settling. The academic paper can be seen here . items.rss_description: Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay nearly $30 million to settle claims by President Donald Trump’s administration that the defense contractor discriminated against white workers through its workplace diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies, according to two federal agencies. The …
items.extracted_text: Lockheed Paying $30M to Settle Trump Administration Claims Over DEI Practices Article 0 Comments Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay nearly $30 million to settle claims by President Donald Trump’s administration that the defense contractor discriminated against white workers through its workplace diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies, according to two federal agencies. The settlements announced late Tuesday include $22 million to resolve claims that Lockheed falsely certified its compliance with anti-discrimination laws to receive federal contracts while favoring non-white workers in hiring, promotion and pay decisions. The company will also pay $7.5 million to more than 1,000 employees affected by its practices, according to the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which enforces federal laws banning workplace discrimination. Lockheed in a statement denied the allegations and said it agreed to the settlements to avoid prolonged litigation. “We did not admit liability, determining it would be best for all involved to put these matters behind us so we can remain focused on our critical national security mission,” the company said. The settlement is the latest in a string of similar deals the Department of Justice has reached with other major U.S. companies including IBM, Accenture and consulting firm Deloitte as the Trump administration seeks to curb DEI in virtually all areas of American life including private employment, government, education and healthcare. The class of workers involved in the EEOC settlement is the largest to be publicly announced in a case by the agency involving DEI practices, the commission said on Wednesday. Federal law “protects every worker from employment discrimination on the basis of race — and that protection does not yield when discriminatory decisions are framed as diversity initiatives,” EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, a Trump appointee, said in a statement. The agencies allege that Lockheed in 2021 launched an incentive program known as Compensation Adder that awarded the top 20% of employees in each business area with additional annual pay increases. Managers were initially told to use merit-based criteria, but Lockheed pressured some of them to reconsider their selections because of the demographics of the workers chosen, the Justice Department claimed. The agencies also alleged that Lockheed took race or sex into account when making hiring and promotion decisions in order to meet internal diversity goals and for training and mentoring opportunities. The Justice Department’s claims stemmed from a whistleblower lawsuit filed last year by a former vice president at Lockheed, Tim Booher, who will receive a $4.4 million payout, the department said. Booher is now an advisor to the Pentagon, according to his profile on the networking site LinkedIn. items.title: Lockheed to pay $30M to settle Trump administration claims over DEI
items.original_title: Lockheed to pay $30M to settle Trump administration claims over DEI
items.rss_title: Lockheed to pay $30M to settle Trump administration claims over DEI
items.rss_description: Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay nearly $30 million to settle claims by President Donald Trump’s administration that the defense contractor discriminated against white workers through its workplace diversity, equity and inclusion policies, according to two federal agencies.
items.extracted_text: The settlements announced late Tuesday include $22 million to resolve claims that Lockheed falsely certified its compliance with anti-discrimination laws to receive federal contracts while favoring non-white workers in hiring, promotion and pay decisions. The company will also pay $7.5 million to more than 1,000 employees affected by its practices, according to the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which enforces federal laws banning workplace discrimination. Lockheed in a statement denied the allegations and said it agreed to the settlements to avoid prolonged litigation. “We did not admit liability, determining it would be best for all involved to put these matters behind us so we can remain focused on our critical national security mission,” the company said. The settlement is the latest in a string of similar deals the Department of Justice has reached with other major U.S. companies, including IBM, Accenture and consulting firm Deloitte, as the Trump administration seeks to curb DEI in virtually all areas of American life, including private employment, government, education and healthcare. The class of workers involved in the EEOC settlement is the largest to be publicly announced in a case by the agency involving DEI practices, the commission said on Wednesday. Federal law “protects every worker from employment discrimination on the basis of race — and that protection does not yield when discriminatory decisions are framed as diversity initiatives,” EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, a Trump appointee, said in a statement. The agencies allege that Lockheed in 2021 launched an incentive program known as Compensation Adder that awarded the top 20% of employees in each business area with additional annual pay increases. Managers were initially told to use merit-based criteria, but Lockheed pressured some of them to reconsider their selections because of the demographics of the workers chosen, the Justice Department claimed. The agencies also alleged that Lockheed took race or sex into account when making hiring and promotion decisions in order to meet internal diversity goals and for training and mentoring opportunities. The Justice Department’s claims stemmed from a whistleblower lawsuit filed last year by a former vice president at Lockheed, Tim Booher, who will receive a $4.4 million payout, the department said. Mr. Booher is now an advisor to the Pentagon, according to his profile on the networking site LinkedIn. items.extracted_text: AI-Powered Insurance Startup Kalepa Valued at $470M in New Funding Round Article 0 Comments Insurance startup Kalepa on Oct. 5 said it raised $75 million at a $470 million valuation, as investors bet that AI solutions can speed up the slow, data-heavy work of pricing risk and writing policies. Growth equity firm Updata Partners led the Series B round, with participation from IA Ventures and Inspired Capital. Insurers have traditionally relied on time-consuming analysis of vast amounts of data to assess risk and set prices. Some are now betting that AI tools can shorten that work and improve margins, adding to the flurry of AI applications promising to disrupt trillion-dollar white-collar industries. Kalepa, whose customers include major industry players such as W.R. Berkley, Bowhead Specialty and AmRisc, has built an AI-powered platform designed to assist insurance workflows across operations, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. The volume of work running through its platform has grown fourfold over the past year, the insurance startup said, adding that it plans to use the new capital to expand its AI product suite, enter new markets and double its headcount in 2027. Kalepa added that insurers using it have reported over 30% to 60% more premium per underwriter and a 58% reduction i n quote time. “Kalepa already operates across underwriting, operations, pricing, and portfolio management. Newer areas of expansion include insurance product development, reinsurance and distribution,” Paul Monasterio, co-founder and CEO of Kalepa, told Reuters. “Most of our hiring will be in engineering, AI, and commercial roles.” The new Series B round brings the total capital raised by the company to $91 million. In 2021, it had raised $14 million led by Inspired Capital with participation from IA Ventures. Copyright 2026 Reuters. Click for restrictions . items.extracted_text: A $6 Billion Hack Puts Crypto’s Wall Street Rebellion on Trial Article 0 Comments For years, the digital-asset industry has sought to shake up finance by stripping away the intermediaries, delays and controls that govern the movement of money on Wall Street. The pitch: faster transactions, final settlement and fewer middlemen with the power to intervene.But the largest crypto heist on record has exposed the dangers — and limits — of that pitch. A system built to move money without restraint offers few ways to stop it when it is stolen, threatening to cement the Wild West reputation the industry has spent years trying to escape.Tokens stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack could be tracked across public blockchains in real time, but billions of dollars remained beyond the reach of those trying to recover them. Tether and Circle, issuers of the two largest stablecoins, were able to freeze some of the stolen tokens because they retained a form of centralized control that much of crypto was designed to eliminate. Now, as crypto seeks a larger place in American finance, the scale of the theft is stirring unease among market participants over whether the industry has been too quick to discard the checks and delays common in traditional finance. In one corner of crypto, the response is already taking shape. Decentralized-finance provider, Unit, has introduced delays on deposits and withdrawals to give it more time to identify potentially stolen assets. “I don’t want T+1 but maybe T+1 hour,” said Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye, referring to TradFi’s practice of settling trades one day after execution. “The idea is to make settlements longer, with more layers, so that hackers can’t take money out this quickly.” On Wall Street, banks, payment networks and clearinghouses provide opportunities to scrutinize suspicious transfers and, in some circumstances, intervene before funds move beyond reach. Those arrangements are neither foolproof nor always reversible. But they embody a principle that crypto has repeatedly blasted: the ability to interrupt the movement of money can be as important as the ability to move it. Crypto has learned some of Wall Street’s lessons the hard way. The collapse of exchange FTX accelerated demand for third-party custody and arrangements that allow traders to keep collateral away from exchanges. Until then, combining trading, custody and other functions on a single platform had been a familiar feature of the industry. This latest reassessment also comes as the industry is courting institutions whose expectations of financial infrastructure were shaped in traditional markets. “The original ethos of crypto was instant, irreversible transfers onchain, and both centralized and DeFi venues respected that retail-user expectation,” said Joshua Lim, co-head of markets at FalconX. “But crypto’s customer base is changing as more institutions are coming in.” Some of those institutions are less willing to accept the risks that come with irreversible transactions, particularly after a series of exchange hacks over the past year. For them, the ability to stop or reverse a transaction can be as important as the speed at which it settles. Shiliang Tang, managing partner of Monarq Asset Management, sees a distinction between where crypto’s speed is most useful and where traditional safeguards may still have an advantage. Blockchain technology may be well suited to cross-border payments and settlement, he said, while trading could be safer when conducted through traditional financial infrastructure. “Large institutions need to feel their capital cannot be hacked and that things can be rolled back,” he said. Following the security incident at Binance, Unit’s Guardians are introducing a protocol upgrade to deter attempts to move stolen assets through the protocol and to give incident-related intelligence more time to become available. Effective immediately, every Unit deposit and… — Unit (@unitxyz) October 30, 2026 All told, the hack is changing how some decentralized finance developers think about security. Systems built around code that execute transactions automatically are increasingly incorporating restrictions that allow operators more time to respond when something goes wrong. Community members of Aave are now asking for flow limits on the largest lending project in DeFi after the Binance hack. “Security issues have made DeFi more complex, with less fully immutable code and more stopgap safeguards like withdrawal limits that could be regarded as somewhat permissioned,” said Tarun Chitra, chief executive officer of crypto risk modeling firm Gauntlet. Chitra argues that advances in artificial intelligence are adding to the pressure for such controls by making cyberattacks more difficult to contain. Yet restoring oversight and delays is no guarantee of safety. Traditional financial institutions face security weaknesses of their own, and their operating schedules can make it harder to respond outside normal market hours. “Traditional finance’s aging codebases, AI’s ability to reverse-engineer closed-source code, and their inherent lack of 24/7 response has made them vulnerable to hacks as well,” said Chitra, who worked as a quantitative researcher previously. At the same time, AI security is also “pushing towards more 24/7 systems in traditional finance.” Top photo: Pedestrians on Wall Street near the New York Stock Exchange in New York, on Nov. 4. items.original_title: SF Fed: El Niño Poses ‘Meaningful Risk’ of Higher Inflation in 2027
items.rss_title: SF Fed: El Niño Poses ‘Meaningful Risk’ of Higher Inflation in 2027
items.rss_description: The El Niño weather pattern that could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in coming months poses a “meaningful risk” of higher U.S. inflation in 2027 even as it also will likely add to employment, according to research published …
items.extracted_text: SF Fed: El Niño Poses ‘Meaningful Risk’ of Higher Inflation in 2027 Article 0 Comments The El Niño weather pattern that could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in coming months poses a “meaningful risk” of higher U.S. inflation in 2027 even as it also will likely add to employment, according to research published Monday by the San Francisco Federal Reserve. The current El Niño may be among the strongest on record, the World Meteorological Organization projected last month, causing drought in some places, flooding in others and increased heat in many parts of the world. “We estimate that the current episode may have already increased headline price levels about 0.3 percentage point between April and July of this year,” three of the regional Fed bank’s researchers wrote in the latest edition of its Economic Letter. Related: Banks Start Reviewing Loan Terms for Clients in El Niño’s Path “The estimates point to that initial rise fading by the end of this year but then potentially pushing prices up in 2027 by as much as 1 percentage point.” The Fed is grappling with inflation that’s been above its 2% target for more than 5-1/2 years due to a series of shocks, including pandemic-era supply chain disruptions, a sharp increase in tariffs in 2025 and a rise in global oil prices since the war in Iran began early this year. The projection that yet another potential shock could put upward pressure on prices comes as the Fed is also addressing the inflationary impact of demand for AI-related goods and services, and financial conditions that analysts say are not particularly restrictive. The Fed held interest rates steady last week but is widely expected to raise the policy rate in December, and again next year, to tamp down inflation. El Nino’s implications for the U.S. economy are uncertain, wrote San Francisco Fed research associates Molly Arden and Toby Graf, with senior economist Brigitte Roth Tran. Though improved weather forecast quality allows businesses, households and policymakers to be better prepared than in the past, the paper’s authors wrote, global integration of markets means the U.S. economy may be more sensitive than before to foreign shocks. “More recent developments like the disruptions to the fertilizer market, supply chain disruptions in energy markets, and record-setting weather events could also interact with this El Niño in unexpected ways,” they wrote. items.original_title: Verisk: Cargo Theft Losses Rise Despite Drop in Reported Incidents
items.rss_title: Verisk: Cargo Theft Losses Rise Despite Drop in Reported Incidents
items.rss_description: Even as the number of reported cargo thefts fell 25%, the average value of stolen commodities rose 72% through the first nine months of 2026, as thefts of high-value goods pushed up severity, a new report shows. Verisk CargoNet reported …
items.extracted_text: Verisk: Cargo Theft Losses Rise Despite Drop in Reported Incidents Article 0 Comments Even as the number of reported cargo thefts fell 25%, the average value of stolen commodities rose 72% through the first nine months of 2026, as thefts of high-value goods pushed up severity, a new report shows. Verisk CargoNet reported 2,072 supply chain crime incidents through September, down from 2,755 during the same period in 2025. Estimated losses rose 39% to $718.9 million, while the average value of stolen commodities in incidents with documented values rose to $448,456 from $261,115. Verisk CargoNet’s quarterly supply chain risk analysis shows 547 theft incidents across the U.S. and Canada in the third quarter, a 33% decline from the same period last year and a 19% drop from the previous quarter. Ninteen thefts with documented values of $1 million or more occurred during the quarter, up from nine in the third quarter of last year. Many of those thefts involved high-value electronics and data center materials. Related: Verisk: Cargo Theft Losses Hit $304M on Organized Crime Cyber Schemes Fictitious pickups are on the rise. The schemes, in which criminals use deception to obtain shipments, increased from 18% to roughly 25% in the past quarter. Food and beverage remained the most frequently stolen commodity category with 94 incidents, although that was down from 178 incidents in the third quarter of 2025. Nonalcoholic beverages accounted for 22 incidents, followed by meat products (21) and alcoholic beverages (12). Metals were the second most frequently stolen commodity category with 63 incidents. Copper theft accounted for 34 of those incidents. Household goods thefts fell from 95 to 49 incidents, while electronics fell from 69 to 46. Computers and accessories accounted for 20 incidents, down from 24 a year earlier. Personal care and beauty thefts declined from 44 to 39 incidents. California was the state that recorded the most cargo theft incidents during the third quarter at 182. That was down from 261 a year earlier. New Jersey followed (46) and Texas recorded (43) followed. Those three states accounted for 49.5% of all reported thefts during the quarter, according to CargoNet. Los Angeles, San Bernardino and Riverside counties in California were among the areas with high concentrations of theft, along with Harris County, Texas, and Cook County, Illinois. The top targeted location types were warehouses and distribution centers, followed by truck stops, the report shows. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.rss_description: Swiss Re said Thursday it has appointed longtime Aon executive Lori Goltermann to the newly created role of chief commercial officer of Swiss Re Corporate Solutions, its commercial insurance arm, effective Jan. 11, 2027.
items.extracted_text: 11, 2027. Based in Chicago, Ms. Goltermann will oversee the unit’s global commercial strategy and relationships with clients, governments and brokers. She will report to Swiss Re Corporate Solutions CEO Ivan Gonzalez and join its executive committee. Ms. Goltermann, who joined Aon in 1993, held numerous leadership roles at the brokerage, rising to CEO of North America and global regions in 2024. Earlier this year , she was named vice chair and Anne Corona was named North America CEO. Ms. Goltermann is the latest in a series of prominent executive departures from Aon. Former Aon President Eric Andersen left to become CEO of American International Group in June, while Edmund Reese, who succeeded Christa Davies as Aon’s chief financial officer in 2024, stepped down in August. Ms. Goltermann was a 2016 Business Insurance Women to Watch honoree and named an Iconic leader in 2025.
